papers.title: The Endogeneity of Miscalibration: Impossibility and Escape in Scored Reporting
papers.abstract: An agent's probability report is paid for twice: by a strictly proper scoring rule, which rewards accuracy, and by an approval rule for the decision it triggers. An approval rule that is not affine is known to defeat truthful reporting. We show the conflict is built in: whenever perfect screening is attainable, the welfare-maximizing approval rule is never affine. The distortion is predictable: there is a reserve report at which pretending to be the marginal type costs exactly what approval is worth. Approving every report at or above the reserve sorts agents as if their beliefs were observed, under every strictly proper score and for any belief distribution. So does a continuous rule with one corner; under strict feasibility no continuously differentiable rule does. The binding constraint is steepness, not smoothness: a slope-capped rule sorts perfectly if and only if the cap reaches the critical slope, the steepest chord of the pretending cost up to the reserve; below it the welfare loss is cubic in the shortfall. For the Brier, log and power scores, and whenever the pretending cost is convex up to the reserve, the critical slope has a closed form. The instances are AI-agent oversight and marketplace operation.

papers.title: When Good News Fails in Evolution: A Note on Information, Exposure, and Evolutionary Stability
papers.abstract: Good news about a strategy need not translate into evolutionary success. We study how the interaction between information and strategy exposure shapes evolutionary dynamics and equilibrium predictions. We derive the associated population dynamic from a simple revision process in which agents encounter candidate strategies at state-dependent rates and adopt them after receiving favorable payoff signals. We distinguish the monotone likelihood ratio property (MLRP) of signals from effective MLRP, which accounts for exposure relative to population shares and determines whether better-performing strategies grow faster. Random population encounters preserve MLRP and generate payoff-monotone evolution. When exposure sufficiently favors rare strategies, effective MLRP is violated near strict pure Nash equilibria, rendering them unstable. Conversely, when exposure sufficiently favors popular strategies, effective MLRP is violated near non-Nash pure states, allowing them to remain locally stable. Thus, even when signals satisfy MLRP, differences in strategy exposure can reverse their evolutionary implications and alter equilibrium predictions.

papers.title: Moral AI and the Erosion of Its Own Demand
papers.abstract: We study the evolution of human preference frequencies and AI adoption when individuals can choose between a moral AI that rules out defection and an unconstrained AI that preserves discretion. By allowing users to commit to cooperation, moral AI can sustain cooperation even when cooperative preferences are too scarce to do so on their own. But this success has a cost. By turning otherwise dormant cooperative preferences into committed behavior, moral AI exposes its users to exploitation by selfish individuals, causing the population share of conditional cooperators to decline under evolutionary selection. As conditional cooperators become less prevalent, equilibrium adoption eventually converges to zero. Moral AI can therefore be self-liquidating. For initial shares between the moral-AI adoption cutoff and the threshold for cooperation without AI, moral AI generates cooperation while lowering the limiting share of conditional cooperators. Adoption ultimately vanishes, leaving a lower share of the preference type that initially sustained demand for commitment.

papers.title: Folk Theorems for Social Learning
papers.abstract: We study repeated games with purely informational externalities. Each player observes a single conditionally independent signal and then repeatedly takes publicly observed actions to maximize their expected discounted payoff, which depends only on the state and their own action. We show that, when there are sufficiently many players and they are sufficiently patient, there exist equilibria where information is aggregated: the players' payoffs approximate the full-information payoff. This holds even if actions are uninformative under myopic play. Conversely, even if myopic play reveals the state, there also exist equilibria where information is not aggregated: payoffs approximate those under autarky. Our results speak to the range of possible outcomes of social learning games with forward-looking agents.

papers.title: Cognitive Constraints and Misspecification Concern
papers.abstract: We study repeated decision problems in which an agent has cognitive constraints and is concerned that her models might be misspecified. She first uses data to weight candidate models, subject to a cognitive-capacity constraint on the complexity she can process, and then she evaluates choices according to how well they perform under those models. More data need not overcome limited capacity: a statistically inferior but simpler model can remain relevant in the long run. When the constraint binds, evidence that favors models in proportion to their complexity can leave current behavior unchanged while still affecting later responses to data. This constraint eliminates cycles between risky and safe actions when simple models favor safety, and relaxing it can make risky play more attractive initially yet less frequent in the long run. It can also sustain misspecified model classes by suppressing choices that would reveal their errors.

papers.title: A Simple Proof of Koray's Theorem
papers.abstract: In this note, I provide a direct and self-contained proof of Koray's (2000) theorem, by which a neutral and unanimous social choice function is universally self-selective if and only if it is dictatorial. Koray's (2000) original proof relies on results by Sen (1970) and Houthakker (1950) to construct a social welfare function for each alternative set. He then shows that these functions are Paretian and independent of irrelevant alternatives, allowing him to apply Arrow's (1950, 1951) impossibility theorem. Instead, I construct a cyclic preference profile and show that the voter who ranks the chosen alternative first is the dictator on every finite nonempty alternative set.

papers.title: Obvious group manipulations in voting
papers.abstract: We study obvious group manipulation in voting and characterize it as manipulation identifiable from a coalition's option sets alone. Our analysis focuses on two overlapping classes: tops-only rules and rules satisfying the majority criterion, including all Condorcet-consistent rules. On the universal domain with at least three alternatives, a tops-only rule is not obviously manipulable by groups (NOMG) if and only if it is dictatorial. For rules satisfying the majority criterion, NOMG is impossible when $n,m\geq3$, except with four voters and three alternatives. We quantify the coalition sizes behind these restrictions, obtaining sharp bounds for efficient tops-only rules and an exact threshold for majority-criterion rules with odd electorates. In the exceptional configuration, we characterize an interval of NOMG scoring rules containing Borda, which is also Condorcet consistent there. We further characterize NOMG with two alternatives and apply our tops-only characterization to generalized median voter schemes and voting by committees.

papers.title: An Enforcement Foundation for Constrained Equal Awards
papers.abstract: Standard claims problems take claims as given. We ask how rule selection changes when a certified claim can be augmented by a privately known component that is costly to verify. In a binary environment, equal treatment of equals, claim boundedness, and efficiency impose a sharp lower bound on the gain from exaggeration and hence on the expected auditing needed for truthful reporting to be weakly dominant. The constrained equal awards (CEA) rule attains this bound at every report profile through a correlated audit policy. Conversely, every profilewise audit-minimal rule is CEA. The pointwise result also makes CEA the unique admissible rule that minimizes expected verification cost under every prior over true claims.

papers.title: Entry Deterrence with Public Signals: Revisiting the Chain-Store Paradox
papers.abstract: We revisit the classic chain-store paradox by introducing exogenous public signals about the incumbent's private type that arrive each period over a finite horizon. We fully characterize perfect Bayesian equilibria in terms of sequences of reputation cutoffs that increase over time: entrants enter below their cutoff, while the normal incumbent mixes below its cutoff and fights above it. The equilibrium outcome is generically unique. Information arrival dampens the incentive to build a reputation, so full deterrence need not emerge as the horizon grows arbitrarily long, even when the incumbent is very patient. We characterize exactly when there is full deterrence in the limit, along with the limiting equilibrium when there is not.

papers.title: A General Theory of Risk Sharing
papers.abstract: We introduce a new paradigm for risk sharing that generalizes earlier models based on discrete agents and extends them to allow for sharing risk within a continuum of agents. Agents are represented by points of a measure space and have potentially heterogeneous risk preferences modeled by risk measures on a separable probability space. We derive the dual representation of the value function using a Strassen-type theorem for the weak-star topology and provide a characterization of the acceptance set using Aumann integration. These results are illustrated by explicit formulas when risk preferences are within the family of entropic and expected shortfall risk measures, and applications to Pareto efficiency in large markets.

papers.title: The Double-Edged Sword of Information: Revealed versus Hidden Lotteries in School Choice
papers.abstract: In school choice, a lottery number is often used by the matching mechanism to break ties when more students prefer the same school than the number of seats available. In practice, in recent years, the NYC Public Schools started revealing the lottery number to students. Theoretical findings from prior literature suggest that revealing the lottery number strictly improves the number of matches under the deferred acceptance algorithm. However, these theoretical results are based on the over-simplifying assumption that all students share the same preference ranking for schools. In this work, we relax this assumption and allow students to have heterogeneous preference rankings. Under a game-theoretic model where student strategies form a Bayesian Nash equilibrium, we characterize scenarios where revealing the lottery number can either improve or worsen the matching outcome, measured by two metrics of the match rate and social welfare, when students submit preference lists of length one. We further consider revealing partial information about the lottery, and demonstrate non-monotonic effects in the amount of information available to students. From these theoretical results, we identify a mechanism through which lottery revealing deteriorates the overall matching quality: Under the revealed lottery, students with weak preferences but high priorities slightly improve their matching outcome at the cost of increasing congestion and substantially worsening the outcome of students with strong preferences. Using a mean-field approximation, we show via simulations that this mechanism continues to operate when the length of preference lists is greater than one. These theoretical and simulation results together illustrate complex tradeoffs induced by the lottery revealing policy, and we identify students' preference heterogeneity and preference intensity as two key factors in shaping these tradeoffs.

papers.title: Product Returns and the Value of Search Prominence
papers.abstract: Ordered-search models typically make prominence valuable because the first-listed seller receives more traffic. We show that product returns can overturn this logic by changing not only the volume but also the composition of demand. We develop a duopoly model in which consumers inspect products sequentially, learn a coarse match signal through search, discover realized taste only after purchase, and may return the product. With positive consumer hassle costs for product returns and a general taste distribution, optimal consumer behavior is characterized by pre-search inspection, post-search purchase, and retention cutoffs. In a low-hassle, full-refund benchmark with uniformly distributed taste values, the non-prominent firm charges a higher price because consumers who reach it are screened by their experience with the prominent product. Although prominence generates more visits and gross orders, it also exposes the first seller to less-screened, more return-prone demand. When seller-side return losses are sufficiently large, the prominent firm can earn less than its rival while both firms earn positive profits. The reversal also persists on local active pricing branches under small positive hassle costs, small departures from full refunds, and finite oligopoly. Sellers' willingness to pay for prominence therefore depends on how a higher ranking changes both the profits from retained sales and the losses on returned units.

papers.title: Partially Identified Ambiguity
papers.abstract: This paper addresses the normative question of whether one should condition on the data when performing robust Bayesian analysis under partial identification. We provide an ex ante representation of the conditional Gamma-minimax criterion and show that it can violate Aumann plausibility, a set-valued generalization of the rational expectations property. Our main characterization result establishes that Aumann plausibility holds if and only if the decision maker's prior set exhibits partially identified ambiguity. The latter condition requires the prior set to equal the Aumann expectation of a random set of distributions supported on the parameter's identified sets. We interpret these results as suggesting that conditional Gamma-minimax should only be used under partially identified ambiguity. The implications for various robust Bayesian methods are discussed.

papers.title: Demand reduction and initial endowments in consignment auctions
papers.abstract: Consignment auctions, in which bidders first receive free initial endowments of a good and must then consign them to a subsequent uniform price auction, are often used in emissions allowance trading for the environmental regulation of greenhouse gas emissions. We study consignment auctions where many asymmetric bidders have flat demands up to their respective quantity constraints. We first characterize the equilibrium outcome and then examine the effects of initial endowments and total supply. If bidders' initial endowments increase or the total supply decreases, the equilibrium price increases whereas the social welfare and the auctioneer's revenue may increase or decrease. In particular, the revenue may increase even though fewer units remain in the hands of the auctioneer since an increase in initial endowments can prevent the low price equilibrium resulting from demand reduction.

papers.title: Selective Verification in Centralized Admissions: Which Priority Claims Must Be Checked?
papers.abstract: Centralized admissions platforms grant priority based on self-reported facts such as residence, sibling status, or family income, and a false claim can cost another applicant her seat. Verifying every claim before matching is expensive, yet checking only admitted applicants afterward is unsafe: a false claim by an applicant who ends up unmatched may already have triggered a chain of rejections. We show how a platform can check far fewer claims without changing any outcome. A claim matters only if it can move its applicant across a school's admission cutoff, and we give an exact, easily computed test for when this happens. Checking only such claims, and only when they could change a school's tentative choice, reproduces every application, rejection, and assignment of deferred acceptance under full verification. When claims are truthful, checking the highest claimed priority first minimizes checks among such policies at each school decision, and the number of checks never exceeds the school's capacity. Truthful reporting of preferences and eligibility is a weakly dominant strategy, so incentives deliver the conditions under which this audit order is optimal. In simulated markets, the policy cuts verification by 76 percent relative to checking every claim upfront and by 36 percent relative to checking each claim when it first reaches a school. The design principle is to verify decisions, not files.
